newsitem.title: LESOTHO: FEATURE - Rural Lesotho transformed by S.African water scheme.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Rural Lesotho transformed by S.African water scheme.

text.p: Life for thousands of villagers living around Katse Dam, taking shape in Lesotho's remote water-rich mountains to supply the thirsty industries of neighbouring South Africa, will never be the same.

Vula Rafutho, 46, who lives in the small town of Katse that overlooks what will be Africa's highest dam when it is finished late this year, says an age-old way of life has been transformed rapidly in the picturesque Maluti mountain valleys.
Before, little more than a dirt track led over the mountains and was passable only on foot, horse or four-by-four vehicle.

Then a 120 km (70 mile) road was blasted out of the mountain and tarred. Southern Africa's ubiquitous minibus taxis, tourists and workers from across Lesotho and South Africa came to the once quiet valleys.
"Life for everyone here has changed forever. Some are not happy with the dam but others think things have become better and they are happy," Rafutho told Reuters.

The Lesotho Highland project, agreed in 1986 by the tiny kingdom and then-apartheid South Africa, the giant neighbour that surrounds it, is one of the world's biggest water projects but has raised little high-profile environmentalist concern.
RISING WATER SWALLOWS VILLAGES

Pushed out by the dam, villagers have had to set up home higher on the hillsides as the water level rises. Some families have been moved by project authorities into new modern homes above the water level.
Schooling, health facilities and electricity have also been supplied to villagers, often for the first time.

The highland project will eventually feed 70 cubic metres of water per second through about 80 km (50 miles) of tunnels dug into the mountains and then into a river to replenish the distant Vaal Dam, supplier of water to the industrial heartland of Gauteng province around Johannesburg.
Rich farmlands now lie at the foot of the Katse Dam, which can hold 1,950 million cubic metres of water.
More than 13,000 people will be affected by the first two stages of the project.

The project's first subphase, which is almost complete and three months ahead of schedule, includes the construction of the main Katse Dam, 86 km (53 miles) of delivery tunnels, a smaller dam and a hydroelectric plant at nearby Muela.
Not counting the plant, the capital costs -- including interest payments -- of the first phase are expected to be about 9.7 billion rand by completion in March 1998.
Lesotho, whose economy relies heavily on South Africa, was given about 190 million rand by the European Union to build the 72 megawatt hydroelectric plant to make it self-sufficient in power.

The second stage of the project, costing about 7.16 billion rand, will include the building of two smaller dams and delivery tunnels to Katse to boost the dam's initial delivery from 18 cubic metres a second to 30 cubic metres per second.
There are proposals for another three phases which would increase the yield to 70 cubic metres per second, but these have still to be negotiated by Lesotho and South Africa governments.

Compensation and resettlement costs for villagers affected by the first stage totalled 32.4 million rand between 1988 and 1996. The loss of grazing areas and fields have been compensated in kind with deliveries of fodder, maize and pulses.
Project managers are looking at capital expenditure of 250 million rand for the second stage between 1997 and 2003 in direct financial compensation, development and resettlement.
TOURISM, AN ADDED BENEFIT
In the last quarter of 1996 almost 8,000 tourists came to see Katse Dam and the tourism potential has yet to be tapped.
Fears have been raised by South Africa's Water Affairs Minister Kader Asmal that political uncertainty in coup-prone Lesotho could affect water delivery to South Africa.
World Bank President James Wolfensohn said last month that talks with Lesotho on the second phase of the project had been suspended because of such uncertainty after unrest.
However, the chief resident engineer at Katse, Ron Hagen, said Lesotho had a vested interest in the project which was too far advanced for it to be jeopardised by politics.
"I can't see the party in power, or any party which comes into power, foregoing the money they are getting out of this scheme, not for the sake of a few political arguments," he said.
Last September Katse filled to 1,993 metres (6,477 feet) above sea level which was the trigger for the first royalty payment of $55 million to Lesotho, four months ahead of schedule.

Monthly installments on royalties will last for 50 years and the initial payments will represent about five percent of Lesotho's gross national product, which is currently about two billion rand a year.
